lead: A switched network moves data from source to destination through intermediate nodes. Circuit switching first reserves a path for the whole call. Packet switching cuts the message into packets that share links and wait in queues. The first suits a long telephone call that needs a steady rate. The second suits a short file or a web page that arrives in bursts. This chapter shows the three phases of a circuit call, the store-and-forward rule of a packet network, and the delay each adds.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.6 to know which layer holds packets and which holds the call.

blocks.text: A circuit-switched network reserves a path before any data moves. The call has three phases. Setup: the source asks the network for a path, and each switch reserves capacity on its outgoing link. Data transfer: bits flow at a fixed rate along the reserved path. Teardown: the switches release the capacity after the call ends. The telephone network works this way.

Inside one link, the provider multiplexes many calls. FDM gives each call a frequency band. TDM gives each call a repeating time slot. Either way, the call sees a constant rate and a fixed delay, because no other call can take its share. That is why voice sounds steady. The cost is waste: when the caller is silent, the reserved slot or band carries nothing, and no other user can borrow it. Billing usually follows time and distance.

blocks.where: T<sub>circuit</sub> is the total time from request to release (s); t<sub>setup</sub> is the setup time (s); B is the number of bits in the message (bits); R is the reserved rate (bits/s); t<sub>teardown</sub> is the teardown time (s). This ignores propagation delay. In the figure, setup is 3 s, data lasts 12 s and teardown is 5 s, so the call occupies 20 s.

blocks.text: A packet-switched network cuts the message into packets. Each packet carries a header with the source and destination address, a sequence number, and error checks. A router receives the whole packet, stores it, reads the header, and forwards it on the best link. This is store-and-forward: the packet must fully arrive before it leaves. The delay therefore grows with the number of hops.

Links are shared by statistical multiplexing. A user sends only when it has data, and can use the full link rate for a short burst. When many bursts arrive together, packets wait in a queue. Queuing adds variable delay, called jitter. Packets may also take different paths and arrive out of order. The header is overhead: a 1,000-byte packet may carry 40 bytes of header and only 960 bytes of user data.

Two flavours exist. In a datagram network, each packet is routed on its own, as in IP. In a virtual circuit network, setup fixes a path and gives each packet a short label, but no bandwidth is reserved. The path is fixed; the rate is not.

blocks.where: T<sub>packet</sub> is the time from the first bit sent to the last bit received (s); N is the number of packets; k is the number of links; L is the packet size (bits); R is the link rate (bits/s). This assumes all packets are ready, and ignores headers, queuing and propagation.

blocks.text: Circuit switching pays a setup cost but gives a steady rate and low jitter. Packet switching pays no setup for a short transfer, shares capacity better, but adds per-packet headers and variable delay. For a long voice call, circuit switching is a good match. For a short file, a web page, or a bursty sensor reading, packet switching wins because the setup would dominate.

The worked example below shows the crossover. A short 1 MB file needs only 8 s of data time; a 0.5 s setup twice is a large fraction of the total. For a one-hour call, the same setup is negligible. So the choice depends on the holding time and on how bursty the traffic is. The design of the switch fabric and the full multiplexing hierarchy are in Unit 2.

figure.caption: The circuit lane pays 0.5 s of setup before its 8 s of data, then 0.5 s of teardown, ending at 9 s. The packet lane starts at once, sends all 1,000 packets of 8 ms in 8 s, and the last packet's two extra hops add only 16 ms, so it ends at 8.016 s.

spec.aria: Two timelines on a 0 to 9 second axis: the circuit bar is split into a 0.5 s setup, an 8 s data phase and a 0.5 s teardown, totalling 9 s; the packet bar runs from 0 to 8.016 s with no setup or teardown, so it finishes slightly earlier.

examples.question: A 1 MB file crosses three links of 1 Mbps each. Ignore headers, queuing and propagation. (a) Circuit switching with 0.5 s setup and 0.5 s teardown. (b) Packet switching with 1,000-byte packets. Find the total time for each.
steps: Convert the file: 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes = 8,000,000 bits = 8 Mbit.
Sending the whole file over one 1 Mbps link takes 8,000,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 8 s.
Circuit switching: total = setup + data + teardown = 0.5 + 8 + 0.5 = 9 s.
Packet switching: each packet is 1,000 bytes = 8,000 bits. One packet over one link takes 8,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.008 s = 8 ms.
The last packet finishes leaving the source after 1,000 × 8 ms = 8 s. It then needs two more hops, each 8 ms, so add 2 × 8 ms = 16 ms.
examples.answer: Circuit switching takes 9 s; packet switching takes 8.016 s. Packet switching wins here because setup dominates for a short transfer.
examples.check:
file_bytes = 1_000_000
rate = 1_000_000
setup = 0.5
teardown = 0.5
data_time = file_bytes * 8 / rate
circuit_total = setup + data_time + teardown
packet_bytes = 1_000
packet_bits = packet_bytes * 8
per_link = packet_bits / rate
num_packets = file_bytes / packet_bytes
packet_total = num_packets * per_link + 2 * per_link
print(circuit_total)
print(packet_total)

traps: Charging setup and teardown to every packet. They happen once per call, not once per packet.
Forgetting store-and-forward: a router waits for the whole packet before sending it, so delay grows with hops. Do not use only one link time for a multi-hop path.
Mixing virtual circuit with circuit switching. A virtual circuit fixes the path but does not reserve bandwidth, so queuing still occurs.
Using 1 MB = 2²⁰ bytes when the question uses decimal MB. 1 MB here is 10⁶ bytes = 8×10⁶ bits. State the convention.
Adding propagation delay when the question says ignore it. Read the assumptions before you add terms.

quiz.q: Name the three phases of a circuit-switched call.
Why does a circuit-switched call waste capacity when the caller is silent?
quiz.a: The network has reserved a fixed frequency band or time slot for that call. Silence carries no data, but no other user can borrow the reserved share.

quiz.q: A 2 MB file crosses two links of 2 Mbps each. Circuit setup is 1 s and teardown is 1 s. Packet size is 1,000 bytes. Ignore overhead, queuing and propagation. Find the total time for circuit switching and for packet switching.
quiz.a: 2 MB = 16,000,000 bits. One-link data time = 16,000,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 8 s. Circuit total = 1 + 8 + 1 = 10 s. Packets: 2,000 packets of 8,000 bits. Per link = 8,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 0.004 s. Packet total = 2,000 × 0.004 + 1 × 0.004 = 8.004 s.

quiz.q: A video call needs steady delay; a file download is bursty. Which switching suits each, and why?
quiz.a: The video call suits circuit switching because the reserved path gives a constant rate and low jitter. The file download suits packet switching because it is bursty, needs no setup, and can use idle capacity; variable delay does not hurt a file.

quiz.q: What does store-and-forward mean at a router?
quiz.a: The router receives the whole packet into its buffer, reads the header, and only then sends the packet on the next link.

quiz.q: A packet is 1,500 bytes and the link rate is 10 Mbps. Find the transmission time of the packet on that link.
Why can packets arrive out of order in a datagram network, and what field helps the receiver fix the order?
quiz.a: Each packet is routed on its own, so different packets may take different paths and face different queuing delays. A sequence number in the header lets the receiver put them back in order.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern providers run MPLS and segment routing, which borrow the virtual-circuit label idea inside packet networks. Data centres use leaf-spine fabrics where all links are packet-switched. Software-defined networking lets a controller choose paths per flow. 5G separates control and user planes and can mix circuit-like bearers with packet transport. Search next for MPLS labels, segment routing, and 5G network slicing.
